citation.title: Fast computation of exact confidence intervals for randomized experiments with binary outcomes

standing_assumptions:
Finite-population, design-based setting: the $n$ subjects and their binary potential outcomes are fixed and the only randomness is the complete randomization of $m$ subjects to treatment (plus, where stated, independent Monte Carlo draws and, in Section 6, a missingness vector). Printed and PDF page numbers coincide (Journal of Econometrics 251 (2025) 106056). Transcribed from the page images.

(S1) Tables and count vectors, Section 2.1, p. 5: 'Let $\mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ denote the positive integers. We consider a group of $n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ subjects who undergo an experiment with a binary outcome. We let $m$ denote the number of subjects assigned to the treatment group. Then $n - m$ subjects are assigned to control. We let $[\![a,b]\!]$ denote the set $\{k \in \mathbb{Z} : a \le k \le b\}$. A potential outcome table is any vector $\boldsymbol{w} \in \{(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)\}^n$. (2.1) Letting $\boldsymbol{w}_i = (w_i(1), w_i(0))$ for $i \in [\![1,n]\!]$, the coordinate $w_i(1)$ denotes the outcome for the $i$th subject under treatment, and $w_i(0)$ denotes the outcome under control. We use $\boldsymbol{y}$ to denote the potential outcome table for the subjects in the experiment, which is a fixed (but unknown) ground truth. For every table $\boldsymbol{w}$, we let the corresponding count vector $\boldsymbol{v} = \boldsymbol{v}(\boldsymbol{w}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$ be defined by $\boldsymbol{v} = (v_{11}, v_{10}, v_{01}, v_{00})$, $v_{ab} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} \mathbb{1}\{\boldsymbol{w}_j = (a,b)\}$. (2.2)'

(S2) Randomization and observed data, p. 5: 'Consider the random vector $\boldsymbol{Z} = (Z_1, Z_1, \ldots, Z_n) \in \{0,1\}^n$ (2.3) whose distribution is uniform over the set $\mathcal{Z}(n) = \{\boldsymbol{z} \in \{0,1\}^n : \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m\}$. (2.4) Here, the indices $i$ such that $Z_i = 1$ represent the subjects assigned to treatment. The vector of observed experimental outcomes $\boldsymbol{Y} = (Y_j)_{j=1}^{n}$ is then given by $Y_j = Z_j y_j(1) + (1 - Z_j) y_j(0)$. (2.5) We say that a table $\boldsymbol{w}$ is possible given the observed data $\boldsymbol{Y}$ if for every $j \in [\![1,n]\!]$, we have $\boldsymbol{w}_j(1) = Y_j$ if $Z_j = 1$, and $\boldsymbol{w}_j(0) = Y_j$ if $Z_j = 0$. We say that a count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ is possible if it arises from some possible table $\boldsymbol{w}$.' [(2.3) prints $Z_1$ twice; the vector is $(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_n)$: finding P003-E015. The paper's results assume $1 \le m < n$.]

(S3) Estimand and estimator, p. 5: 'The sample average treatment effect for a potential outcome table is defined by $\tau(\boldsymbol{w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(w_j(1) - w_j(0))$. (2.6) The Neyman estimator of $\tau(\boldsymbol{y})$ is given by $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = \sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{Z_j Y_j}{m} - \sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{(1-Z_j)Y_j}{n-m}$. (2.7) This estimator depends on $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ only through the observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$ defined by $\boldsymbol{n} = (n_{11}, n_{10}, n_{01}, n_{00})$, $n_{zy} = \sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbb{1}\{Z_j = z, Y_j = y\}$, (2.8) for $z \in \{0,1\}$ and $y \in \{0,1\}$. For example, $n_{10}$ is the number of subjects in the treatment group with observed outcome 0. Then $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = \frac{n_{11}}{m} - \frac{n_{01}}{n-m}$. We overload the notation slightly and write $T(\boldsymbol{n})$ for the value of the Neyman estimator $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$, if $\boldsymbol{n}$ is the observed count vector for $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$.' 'We write $\log$ for the natural logarithm. When we use the base 2 logarithm, it is always denoted by $\log_2$. Additionally, we often abbreviate probability mass function as pmf.' In terms of the count vector, $\tau(\boldsymbol{v}) = (v_{10} - v_{01})/n$ ((4.2), p. 8: 'any possible count vector $\boldsymbol{v} = (v_{11},v_{10},v_{01},v_{00})$ such that $\tau(\boldsymbol{v}) = \tau_0$ satisfies the equations $v_{11}+v_{10}+v_{01}+v_{00} = n$, $v_{10} - v_{01} = n\tau_0$').

(S4) Candidate values, pp. 5-6: 'As $\boldsymbol{w}$ ranges over all tables, $\tau(\boldsymbol{w})$ takes every value in the set $\mathcal{S}(n) = \{-\frac{n}{n}, -\frac{n-1}{n}, \ldots, \frac{0}{n}, \ldots, \frac{n-1}{n}, \frac{n}{n}\}$, (2.9) which has $2n+1$ elements. After the experiment is completed, the set of $\tau(\boldsymbol{w})$ for $\boldsymbol{w}$ that are possible given the observed data is further restricted to $\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = \{\frac{1}{n}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}(2Z_j - 1)Y_j - m), \ldots, \frac{1}{n}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}(2Z_j-1)Y_j - m + n)\}$, (2.10) which has $n+1$ elements. We observe that $\mathcal{C}$ depends on $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ only through the associated observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n}$.' [$\sum_j (2Z_j-1)Y_j = n_{11} - n_{01}$, so $n\,\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{n}) = [\![n_{11}-n_{01}-m,\; n_{11}-n_{01}-m+n]\!]$.]

(S5) Permutation p-value, Definition 2.1, p. 6: 'Let $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}$ be a random vector independent from $\boldsymbol{Z}$ with the same distribution, and let $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}}$ be the vector with entries $\widetilde{Y}_j = \widetilde{Z}_j w_j(1) + (1 - \widetilde{Z}_j) w_j(0)$. (2.11) We say that $\boldsymbol{w}$ is compatible with observed data $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ at level $1-\alpha$ if $p(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = \mathbb{P}(|T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}) - \tau(\boldsymbol{w})| \ge |T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) - \tau(\boldsymbol{w})|) \ge \alpha$. (2.12) We say that $\boldsymbol{w}$ is compatible with an observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n}$ if (2.12) holds with $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ replaced by $T(\boldsymbol{n})$.' 'Let $\boldsymbol{v}$ denote the count vector associated with $\boldsymbol{w}$, as defined in (2.2), and let $\boldsymbol{n}$ be as in (2.8). Then it is straightforward to see that $p(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ depends on $(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ only through the count vectors $\boldsymbol{n}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$. This motivates the shorthand $p(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{n}) = p(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$.' [The probability in (2.12) is over $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}$ alone, with $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ held fixed.] Algorithm 2.2, p. 6: 'A permutation test takes as inputs $\alpha \in (0,1)$, a count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$, and a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$. It returns a binary decision, accept or reject, as follows. The algorithm computes $p(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{n})$ by direct enumeration of all $\binom{n}{m}$ elements of the set $\mathcal{Z}(n)$ (defined in Eq. (2.4)), over which $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}$ is uniformly distributed. If $p(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{n}) \ge \alpha$, it accepts. Otherwise, it rejects.'

(S6) The interval $\mathcal{I}_\alpha$, p. 6: 'Given an observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n}$, set $\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{n}) = \{(i,j,k,l) : i \in [\![0,n_{11}]\!], j \in [\![0,n_{10}]\!], k \in [\![0,n_{01}]\!], l \in [\![0,n_{00}]\!]\}$. (2.13) We define vectors $\boldsymbol{v}(i,j,k,l)$ in the following way. Given $(i,j,k,l) \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{n})$, set $\boldsymbol{v}(i,j,k,l) = (i+k,\; n_{11}-i+l,\; n_{01}-k+j,\; n_{10}+n_{00}-j-l)$. (2.14)' '[...] the collection of $\boldsymbol{v}(i,j,k,l)$ such that $(i,j,k,l) \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{n})$ is exactly the set of count vectors $\boldsymbol{v}$ possible given the observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n}$.' 'Algorithm 2.3. This algorithm takes as input $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$. It returns an interval $\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}) = [L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}), U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})]$. By directly enumerating of all elements of $\mathcal{T}$, and applying Algorithm 2.2 to each one, compute the set $\mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{n}) = \{\tau(\boldsymbol{v}(i,j,k,l)) : (i,j,k,l) \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{n}) \text{ and Algorithm 2.2 accepts } \boldsymbol{v}(i,j,k,l)\}$. (2.15) Return $U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}) = \max(\mathcal{K})$ and $L_\alpha = \min(\mathcal{K})$.' 'Then using Algorithm 2.3, we define $\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = [L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}), U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})]$ (2.16) by setting $\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = \mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})$.' [The paper does not say what is returned if $\mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{n})$ is empty, and it shows that $\mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{n})$ is non-empty only for balanced designs, where it contains $T(\boldsymbol{n})$ by Lemma 3.1. A formal statement about an unbalanced design must either prove non-emptiness or fix a convention; for coverage statements, data with empty $\mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{n})$ count as not covering.]

(S7) Cited lemmas, p. 7: 'Lemma 2.4 (Li and Ding, 2016, Theorem 1). A potential outcome table $\boldsymbol{w}$ with count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ is possible given an observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n}$ if and only if $\max(0,\; n_{11}-v_{10},\; v_{11}-n_{01},\; v_{11}+v_{01}-n_{10}-n_{01}) \le \min(v_{11},\; n_{11},\; v_{11}+v_{01}-n_{01},\; n-v_{10}-n_{01}-n_{10})$. (2.17)' 'Lemma 2.5 (Li and Ding, 2016, Theorem A.4). Suppose $n = 2m$. Fix $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and observed data $\boldsymbol{Y}$ and $\boldsymbol{Z}$. For every $\tau_0 \in \mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) \cap \mathcal{C}$, there exists a possible potential outcome table $\boldsymbol{w}$ such that $\tau(\boldsymbol{w}) = \tau_0$ and $p(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) \ge \alpha$.'

(S8) Balanced exact algorithm, p. 8: 'Algorithm 4.3. This algorithm takes as input $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$. It returns an interval $[L^{(1)}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}), U^{(1)}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})]$. We give only the steps for finding $U^{(1)}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})$, since finding $L^{(1)}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})$ is analogous. We perform a binary search using a function $f : [\![nT(\boldsymbol{n}),\, n\max(\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{n}))]\!] \to \{0,1\}$ defined below. The precise definition of this binary search is given as Algorithm B.1 in Appendix B.1. Given an input $x$, the function $f$ returns 0 if $x/n$ is compatible with the vector $\boldsymbol{n}$, and 1 otherwise, where the compatibility of a given $\tau_0 \in \mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{n})$ is determined through the following steps. 1. Initialize $j \leftarrow 0$. 2. If $j \le n$, perform the following steps. (a) Construct a count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ as follows (recall Eq. (2.2)). Let $v_{10}$ be a free parameter, and set $v_{11} = j - v_{10}$. Then (solving Eq. (4.2)) we set $v_{01} = v_{10} - n\tau_0$, $v_{00} = n - j - v_{10} + n\tau_0$. (4.4) (b) Find the smallest $v_{10}$ that leads to a possible table $\boldsymbol{v}$ given the observed data $\boldsymbol{n}$. This can be done in constant time using Lemma B.3, stated in Appendix B.1 below. If no value of $v_{10}$ leads to a possible table, set $j \leftarrow j+1$ and go to (2). (c) Permutation test the count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ coming from the choice of $v_{10}$ in the previous step using Algorithm 2.2 with the given value of $\alpha$. If $\boldsymbol{v}$ is accepted, return that $\tau_0$ is compatible. If $\boldsymbol{v}$ is rejected and $v_{10} \ge 1$ or $v_{01} \ge 1$, set $j \leftarrow j+1$ and go to (2). If $\boldsymbol{v}$ is rejected and $v_{10} = v_{01} = 0$, additionally permutation test the count vector given by $v_{10} = 1$. If it is possible and accepted, terminate the algorithm and declare $\tau_0$ compatible. Otherwise, set $j \leftarrow j+1$ and go to (2). 3. Return that $\tau_0$ is incompatible.'

(S9) Binary search and possibility along a line, Appendix B.1, p. 20: 'Algorithm B.1. This binary search algorithm takes as input $k_1, k_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that $k_2 > k_1$, and a function $f : [\![k_1,k_2]\!] \to \{0,1\}$ such that $f(x) = 0$ if $x \le r$ and $f(x) = 1$ if $x > r$, where $r \in [\![k_1 - 1, k_2]\!]$ is unknown. The algorithm returns $r$ through the following steps. 1. Initialize $a \leftarrow k_1$ and $b \leftarrow k_2$. 2. Set $c \leftarrow \lfloor (a+b)/2 \rfloor$ and evaluate $f(c)$. If $f(c) = 0$, set $a \leftarrow c$. If $f(c) = 1$, set $b \leftarrow c$. 3. Repeat the previous step until $b = a+1$. In this case, return $a$ if $a > k_1$ and $b < k_2$. If $a = k_1$, evaluate $f(k_1)$ and return $k_1 - 1$ if $f(k_1) = 1$, and $k_1$ if $f(k_1) = 0$. If $b = k_2$, evaluate $f(k_2)$, and return $k_2$ if $f(k_2) = 0$ and $k_2 - 1$ if $f(k_2) = 1$.' 'Lemma B.2. Algorithm B.1 terminates in at most $\lfloor \log_2(k_2 - k_1 + 1) + 2 \rfloor$ evaluations of $f$.' 'Lemma B.3. Fix $j, v_{10} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ and $\tau_0 \in \mathcal{C}$, and consider the potential outcome vector $\boldsymbol{v} = (j - v_{10},\; v_{10},\; v_{10} - n\tau_0,\; n - j - v_{10} + n\tau_0)$. (B.1) Given observed data $\boldsymbol{n}$, a necessary condition for $\boldsymbol{v}$ to be possible is that all of the following inequalities hold: $j \ge n\tau_0 + n_{01}$, $j \ge n_{11}$, $n \ge j + n_{10}$, $n_{11} + n\tau_0 + n_{10} + n_{01} \ge j$. (B.2) In this case, the possible values of $v_{10}$ are given by the interval $\max(0,\; n\tau_0,\; j - n_{11} - n_{01},\; n_{11} + n_{01} + n\tau_0 - j) \le v_{10} \le \min(j,\; n_{11} + n_{00},\; n_{10} + n_{01} + n\tau_0,\; n + n\tau_0 - j)$, (B.3) which may be empty.'

(S10) Balanced Monte Carlo algorithm, Section 4.2, p. 9: 'Given a count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$, we define $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}} = \widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}(\boldsymbol{v})$ as the potential outcome table such that $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}_j = (1,1)$, $j = 1,\ldots,v_{11}$; $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}_j = (1,0)$, $j = v_{11}+1,\ldots,v_{11}+v_{10}$; $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}_j = (0,1)$, $j = v_{11}+v_{10}+1,\ldots,v_{11}+v_{10}+v_{01}$; $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}_j = (0,0)$, $j = v_{11}+v_{10}+v_{01}+1,\ldots,n$. (4.5)' 'Algorithm 4.4. Take as input $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $\varepsilon \in [0,\alpha)$, $K \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, a count vector $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$, and a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$. The algorithm will return a binary decision, either accept or reject. Let $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{Z}^{(K)}$ be a sequence of independent, identically distributed random vectors, with common distribution equal to that of $\boldsymbol{Z}$. Define random variables $V_1,\ldots,V_K$ by $V_i = \mathbb{1}(|T(\boldsymbol{n}^{(i)}) - \tau(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}})| \ge |T(\boldsymbol{n}) - \tau(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}})|)$, $i \in [\![1,K]\!]$, (4.6) where $\boldsymbol{n}^{(i)}$ is the outcome count vector corresponding to $(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(i)},\boldsymbol{Z}^{(i)})$, with $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(i)}$ defined by $Y^{(i)}_j = Z^{(i)}_j \widetilde{w}_j(1) + (1 - Z^{(i)}_j)\widetilde{w}_j(0)$ (4.7) for all $j \in [\![1,n]\!]$. Set $S = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K} V_i$. (4.8) Simulate a realization of $S$ by simulating realizations of the $K$ variables $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{Z}^{(K)}$, and constructing the $V_i$ and $S$ accordingly. Return the decision accept if $S + \varepsilon \ge \alpha$, and return the decision reject otherwise.' 'Algorithm 4.5. This algorithm takes as input $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $\varepsilon \in [0,\alpha)$, and a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$. It returns an interval $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon,K}(\boldsymbol{n}) = [L_{\alpha,\varepsilon,K}(\boldsymbol{n}), U_{\alpha,\varepsilon,K}(\boldsymbol{n})]$. The algorithm is identical to Section 4, except every use of an exact permutation test (Algorithm 2.2) is replaced with an approximate permutation test with the given parameters (Algorithm 4.4). A new set of independent vectors $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{Z}^{(k)}$ is generated for each approximate permutation test (independently of the permutation vectors used for any previous tests).' 'Given observed data $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ we define the interval $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon,K}(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ to be the interval $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,\varepsilon,K}(\boldsymbol{n})$ returned by Algorithm 4.5 for the observed count vector $\boldsymbol{n}$ corresponding to $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$.' ['identical to Section 4' means identical to Algorithm 4.3, and $K \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is also an input: finding P003-N005, cross-references.]

(S11) General Monte Carlo algorithm, Section 5.1, pp. 10-13: estimand $\theta : \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2} \to \mathbb{R}$ and test statistic $R : \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2} \times \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2} \to \mathbb{R}$ ('Estimands $\theta$ will take potential outcome count vectors $\boldsymbol{v}$ as arguments, and test statistics $R$ will take pairs $(\boldsymbol{n},\boldsymbol{v})$ of observed count vectors $\boldsymbol{n}$ and count vectors $\boldsymbol{v}$ as arguments'). 'Algorithm 5.1. Take as input $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $K \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, an estimand $\theta$, a test statistic $R$, a count vector $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$, and a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$. The algorithm will return a binary decision, either accept or reject, the value $\theta(\boldsymbol{v})$, and $K$ vectors lying in $\mathcal{Z}(n)$. Let $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{Z}^{(K)}$ be a sequence of independent, identically distributed random vectors, with common distribution equal to that of $\boldsymbol{Z}$. Define random variables $V_1,\ldots,V_K$ by $V_i = \mathbb{1}(|R(\boldsymbol{n}^{(i)},\boldsymbol{v})| \ge |R(\boldsymbol{n},\boldsymbol{v})|)$, $i \in [\![1,K]\!]$, (5.1) where $\boldsymbol{n}^{(i)}$ is the outcome count vector corresponding to $(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(i)},\boldsymbol{Z}^{(i)})$, with $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(i)}$ defined by $Y^{(i)}_j = Z^{(i)}_j\widetilde{w}_j(1) + (1 - Z^{(i)}_j)\widetilde{w}_j(0)$ (5.2) for all $j \in [\![1,n]\!]$, and we recall the definition of $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{w}}$ from Eq. (4.5). Set $S = \frac{1}{K+1}(1 + \sum_{i=1}^{K} V_i)$. (5.3) [...] Return the decision accept if $S > \alpha$, and return the decision reject otherwise. Also return $\theta(\boldsymbol{v})$ and the realized values of $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(1)},\ldots,\boldsymbol{Z}^{(K)}$.' 'Algorithm 5.3. This algorithm takes as input $\alpha \in (0,1)$, $K \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, a vector $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$, an estimand $\theta$, and a test statistic $R$. It returns a confidence set $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K}$. We initialize $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K} \leftarrow \varnothing$. For every $\tau_0 \in \mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{n})$, in descending order from $\max(\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{n}))$, we perform the following steps. 1. Initialize $j \leftarrow 0$. 2. If $j \le n$, perform the following steps. (a) Construct a count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ as follows (recall Eq. (2.2)). Let $v_{10}$ be a free parameter, and set $v_{11} = j - v_{10}$. Then (solving Eq. (4.2)) we set $v_{01} = v_{10} - n\tau_0$, $v_{00} = n - j - v_{10} + n\tau_0$. (5.16) (b) Find the smallest $v_{10}$ that leads to a possible table $\boldsymbol{v}$ given the observed data $\boldsymbol{n}$. This can be done in constant time using Lemma B.3. If no value of $v_{10}$ leads to a possible table, set $j \leftarrow j+1$ and return to (2). (c) Monte Carlo permutation test the count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ coming from the choice of $v_{10}$ in the previous step using Algorithm 5.1 with the given values of $\alpha$, $K$, $\theta$, and $R$. If $\boldsymbol{v}$ is accepted, set $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K} \leftarrow \mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K} \cup \{\theta(\boldsymbol{v})\}$ using the returned value of $\theta(\boldsymbol{v})$. (d) Using the returned decision and $K$ samples $\boldsymbol{Z}^{(i)}$ from the previous step, use the procedure described below in Section 5.1.1 to return a set $\mathcal{J}(\boldsymbol{v}) \subset \mathbb{R}$. (e) Set $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K} \leftarrow \mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K} \cup \mathcal{J}(\boldsymbol{v})$.' Section 5.1.1, p. 12: 'For all $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, denote $\boldsymbol{v}_k = (v_{11}-k,\; v_{10}+k,\; v_{01}+k,\; v_{00}-k)$ (5.17) and let $\mathcal{L} = \{\boldsymbol{v}_k : k \in [\![1,n]\!], \boldsymbol{v}_k \text{ is possible given } \boldsymbol{n}\}$. (5.18)'; the draws for $\boldsymbol{v}$ are converted by the random update (5.19)-(5.26) into draws for $\boldsymbol{v}' = \boldsymbol{v} + (-1,1,1,-1)$ (printed '$(-1,1,1-1)$'), iterated along $\mathcal{L}$; $\mathcal{V}$ is the set of $\boldsymbol{v}_k \in \mathcal{L}$ that 'are both possible and would be accepted by an application of Algorithm 5.1', and $\mathcal{J} = \{\theta(\boldsymbol{v}) : \boldsymbol{v} \in \mathcal{V}\}$ (5.27). 'As in (2.16), we use $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K}(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ as shorthand for $\mathcal{I}_{\alpha,K}(\boldsymbol{n})$, where $\boldsymbol{n}$ is the count vector for $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$.'

(S12) Missing data, Section 6, pp. 13-14: 'we suppose that instead of observing $(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$, the experimenter observes $(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})$, where $\boldsymbol{M} \in \{-1,0,1\}^n$, $M_i = -J_i + (1 - J_i)Y_i$, (6.1) and $\boldsymbol{J} \in \{1,0\}^n$. Here $\boldsymbol{J}$ is a random variable which may have an arbitrary distribution, and in particular may depend on $\boldsymbol{Y}$ and $\boldsymbol{Z}$. The indices $i$ such that $J_i = 0$ denote realized outcomes that are observed, while those such that $J_i = 1$ indicate missing data. Hence, we have $M_i = -1$ if the realized outcome for the $i$th subject is not observed.' 'Definition 6.1. Given a observed data $(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})$, we define the vector $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)} \in \{0,1\}^n$ by $Y^{(+)}_i = 1$ if $J_i = 1$ and $Z_i = 1$, $Y^{(+)}_i = 0$ if $J_i = 1$ and $Z_i = 0$, $Y^{(+)}_i = M_i$ if $J_i = 0$. Similarly, we define $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)} \in \{0,1\}^n$ by $Y^{(-)}_i = 0$ if $J_i = 1$ and $Z_i = 1$, $Y^{(-)}_i = 1$ if $J_i = 1$ and $Z_i = 0$, $Y^{(-)}_i = M_i$ if $J_i = 0$. Finally, for $\alpha \in (0,1)$, we set $\mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z}) = [\min(L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)},\boldsymbol{Z}), T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)},\boldsymbol{Z})),\; \max(U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}), T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}))]$. (6.2)'

(S13) Symmetric-decreasing pmfs, Appendix A, p. 18: 'For $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, we denote $k^{-1}\mathbb{Z} = \{\frac{j}{k} : j \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, $k^{-1}(2\mathbb{Z}) = \{\frac{2j}{k} : j \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, $k^{-1}(2\mathbb{Z}+1) = \{\frac{2j+1}{k} : j \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. (A.1) Definition A.1. Let $f : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ be a probability mass function. We say that $f$ is symmetric about $k_0$ for some $k_0 \in 2^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ if $f(k_0 - x) = f(k_0 + x)$ for all $x \in 2^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ such that $k_0 + x \in \mathbb{Z}$. (A.2) If $f$ is symmetric about $k_0$, we say that $f$ is decreasing away from $k_0$ if $f(k_0 + y) \le f(k_0 + x)$ for all $x, y \in 2^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ such that $y > x$ and $k_0 + x, k_0 + y \in \mathbb{Z}$. (A.3) We now suppose that $\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} k f(k)$ converges absolutely, so that the mean of the distribution corresponding to $f$ exists. In this case, we say that $f$ is symmetric-decreasing (abbreviated SD) if $f$ is symmetric about $k_0 = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} k f(k)$, and decreasing away from $k_0$. Given $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ and $k_0 \in 2^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$, we say that a probability mass function $f : k^{-1}\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is symmetric about $k^{-1}k_0 \in (2k)^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$ if the function $g : \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ defined by $g(x) = f(kx)$ is symmetric about $k_0$. Similarly, we say that $f$ is SD if $g(x) = f(kx)$ is.' 'Recall from (2.1) that $\boldsymbol{w}$ denotes a generic potential outcome table. We use the notation $T(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Z})$ to stand for $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ with $Y$ generated using the potential outcomes $\boldsymbol{w}$ and the treatment assignments given by $\boldsymbol{Z}$. Since this quantity depends on $\boldsymbol{w}$ only through its associated count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$, we also write $T(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{Z})$ for $T(\boldsymbol{n},\boldsymbol{Z})$.' [As printed, (A.3) lacks the restriction $0 \le x$, and the rescaling should be $g(x) = f(x/k)$: finding P003-E006, target P003-T14. Throughout the targets, 'SD' means the corrected definition: symmetric about the mean and non-increasing in the distance from the mean, on the stated lattice. '$T(\boldsymbol{n},\boldsymbol{Z})$' should read '$T(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Z})$' (finding P003-N017), and it is the distribution of $T(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Z})$, not its value at a fixed labeled assignment, that depends on $\boldsymbol{w}$ only through $\boldsymbol{v}$ (finding P003-E015).]

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 6.2 (coverage with missing outcomes, two extremal imputations), as printed, with its proof in Appendix D
canonical_claim.location: p. 14 (PDF p. 14), statement; pp. 13-14 (PDF pp. 13-14), Section 6 definitions; p. 29 (PDF p. 29), proof
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. Proposition 6.2 (p. 14): 'Suppose $m < n \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, and fix potential outcomes $\boldsymbol{y}$ and $\alpha \in (0,1)$. Then $\mathbb{P}(\tau(\boldsymbol{y}) \in \mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})) \ge 1 - \alpha$, (6.3) where the probability is with respect to the variable $\boldsymbol{Z}$.' Here $\boldsymbol{M}$ is given by (6.1) with $\boldsymbol{J} \in \{1,0\}^n$ 'a random variable which may have an arbitrary distribution, and in particular may depend on $\boldsymbol{Y}$ and $\boldsymbol{Z}$', and $\mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z}) = [\min(L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)},\boldsymbol{Z}), T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)},\boldsymbol{Z})),\; \max(U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}), T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}))]$ (6.2) with $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)}$, $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)}$ as in Definition 6.1. 'Remark 6.3. In the balanced case $n = 2m$, Lemma 3.1 implies that the definition of $\mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})$ simplifies to $\mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z}) = [L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(-)},\boldsymbol{Z}), U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z})]$.'
Appendix D (p. 29): 'Proof of Proposition 6.2. First, note that by Proposition 3.2, $\mathbb{P}(\tau(\boldsymbol{y}) \in \mathcal{J}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})) \ge 1 - \alpha$, (D.1) where $\mathcal{J}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z}) = \bigcup_{\boldsymbol{Y}' \in \mathcal{Y}(\boldsymbol{M})} \mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z})$, (D.2) and $\mathcal{Y}(\boldsymbol{M})$ consists of all vectors of realized outcomes $\boldsymbol{Y}'$ compatible with the partially observed vector $\boldsymbol{M}$. To complete the proof of the theorem it then suffices to show that $\mathcal{J}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z}) \subset \mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})$, (D.3) or equivalently, $\mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})^c \subset \mathcal{J}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})^c = \bigcap_{\boldsymbol{Y}' \in \mathcal{Y}(\boldsymbol{M})} \mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z})^c$. (D.4) Fix some $\tau_0 \in \mathcal{I}^{\circ}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{M},\boldsymbol{Z})^c$. We may suppose that $\tau_0 > \max(U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}), T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}))$, (D.5) since the analogous argument in the complementary case is similar. Then we must show that all tables $\boldsymbol{w}$ such that $\tau(\boldsymbol{w}) = \tau_0$ are incompatible with all choices of $(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z})$ with $\boldsymbol{Y}' \in \mathcal{Y}(\boldsymbol{M})$. Fix such a $\boldsymbol{w}$ and a choice of $\boldsymbol{Y}'$. By the definition of $\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)}$, and since $T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z})$ and $T(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z})$ are coupled through $\boldsymbol{Z}$, we have $\tau_0 \ge T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}) \ge T(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z})$. (D.6) Then $\mathbb{P}(|T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}) - \tau_0| \ge |T(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z}) - \tau_0|) \le \mathbb{P}(|T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}) - \tau_0| \ge |T(\boldsymbol{Y}^{(+)},\boldsymbol{Z}) - \tau_0|) < \alpha$, (D.7) so $\boldsymbol{w}$ is incompatible with $(\boldsymbol{Y}',\boldsymbol{Z})$, as desired.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Section 6 set-up, (6.1), Definition 6.1 and (6.2): standing assumption (S12). $\mathcal{Y}(\boldsymbol{M})$ (Appendix D, p. 29): the set of all $\boldsymbol{Y}' \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $Y'_i = M_i$ for every $i$ with $J_i = 0$ (every binary completion of the missing entries). $\mathcal{I}_\alpha$, $L_\alpha$, $U_\alpha$: Algorithm 2.3 and (2.16), standing assumption (S6); the p-value $p$ and 'possible': (S2), (S5); $\tau$, $T$: (S3).
canonical_claim.note: The headline claim P003-H6 as the paper states it. It is false as stated for unbalanced designs (counterexample: target P003-T1); it holds when n = 2m (target P003-T2), and for arbitrary allocation with the completion hull in place of (6.2) (target P003-T3). The first step of the printed proof, (D.1), is correct; the false steps are (D.3) and the last inequality of (D.7). 'With respect to the variable Z' should include the randomness of J (finding P003-E015). Remark 6.4 (fictitious subject for odd n) is a separate statement that the validators confirmed (P003-N009, not confirmed as an error) and is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Algorithm B.1 (binary search) and Lemma B.2, as printed, with the step of the proof of Theorem 4.1 that uses them
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 20). 'Algorithm B.1. This binary search algorithm takes as input $k_1, k_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that $k_2 > k_1$, and a function $f : [\![k_1,k_2]\!] \to \{0,1\}$ such that $f(x) = 0$ if $x \le r$ and $f(x) = 1$ if $x > r$, where $r \in [\![k_1 - 1, k_2]\!]$ is unknown. The algorithm returns $r$ through the following steps. 1. Initialize $a \leftarrow k_1$ and $b \leftarrow k_2$. 2. Set $c \leftarrow \lfloor (a+b)/2 \rfloor$ and evaluate $f(c)$. If $f(c) = 0$, set $a \leftarrow c$. If $f(c) = 1$, set $b \leftarrow c$. 3. Repeat the previous step until $b = a+1$. In this case, return $a$ if $a > k_1$ and $b < k_2$. If $a = k_1$, evaluate $f(k_1)$ and return $k_1 - 1$ if $f(k_1) = 1$, and $k_1$ if $f(k_1) = 0$. If $b = k_2$, evaluate $f(k_2)$, and return $k_2$ if $f(k_2) = 0$ and $k_2 - 1$ if $f(k_2) = 1$.' 'Lemma B.2. Algorithm B.1 terminates in at most $\lfloor \log_2(k_2 - k_1 + 1) + 2 \rfloor$ evaluations of $f$.' 'Proof. Without loss of generality, we may suppose that $k_1 = 1$. Further, by setting $f(x) = 1$ for $x > k_2$, we may consider $f$ as a function on $[\![1, 2^d + 1]\!]$, where $d = \lfloor \log_2(k_2) + 1 \rfloor$ satisfies $2^d \ge k_2$. Then the number of integers in the interval $[a,b]$ after each evaluation of $f$ follows the sequence $2^{d-1}+1, \ldots, 2^1 + 1, 2$ as the algorithm progresses, with a possible additional evaluation of $f$ if $a = 1$ or $b = 2^d + 1$ at the final step. Then at worst $d + 1$ evaluations are needed in total, which proves the theorem.'
The two assertions are: (1) for every input satisfying the stated conditions, the algorithm returns $r$; (2) it does so after at most $\lfloor \log_2(k_2 - k_1 + 1) + 2 \rfloor$ evaluations of $f$.
Use in the proof of Theorem 4.1 (p. 21): 'Then it suffices to show the following two claims. First, that the $f$ given in Algorithm 4.3 satisfies $f(x) = 0$ if $x/n \in \mathcal{J}_\alpha$ and $f(x) = 1$ otherwise. Second, that $f(x)$ can be computed in at most $(n+1)$ permutation tests for every $x \ne 0$, and $2(n+1)$ permutation tests when $x = 0$. In this case, Lemma B.2 shows that the binary search indicated in Algorithm 4.3 will return $U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})$ after performing at most $(n+1)(\lfloor \log_2(n+1) + 2 \rfloor + 1)$ permutation tests, as desired.'
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $[\![a,b]\!]$: standing assumption (S1). Algorithm 4.3, which calls Algorithm B.1 on $[\![nT(\boldsymbol{n}), n\max(\mathcal{C}(\boldsymbol{n}))]\!]$: (S8). In Step 3, 'Repeat the previous step until $b = a+1$' is read as: execute Step 2, then test $b = a+1$, and repeat Step 2 while the test fails; a return ends the algorithm.
canonical_claim.note: As printed both assertions fail on the two-point domain k2 = k1 + 1 (target P003-T4), and the stated input conditions (positive endpoints, k2 > k1) exclude domains that Algorithm 4.3 supplies. According to the validator's argument and exhaustive check (left endpoint 1, lengths 2 to 64), the printed steps do return r on every domain with at least three points. The corrected search is target P003-T5.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 3.1 (in a balanced design the interval contains the Neyman estimate)
canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix A.1, pp. 18-19 (PDF pp. 18-19)
canonical_claim.statement:
'Lemma 3.1. Suppose $n = 2m$. For every $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$, we have $L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}) \le T(\boldsymbol{n}) \le U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})$. (3.1)'
[Here $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\boldsymbol{n}$ is an observed count vector of the balanced design, $n_{11} + n_{10} = n_{01} + n_{00} = m$. The proof shows more: 'Lemma A.3. Let $n = 2m$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$, and fix observed data $\boldsymbol{Y}, \boldsymbol{Z}$. Then there exists a potential outcome table $\boldsymbol{w}$ such that $\tau(\boldsymbol{w}) = T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ is possible given $\boldsymbol{Y}, \boldsymbol{Z}$' (count vector $\boldsymbol{v} = (0,\; n_{11} + n_{00},\; n_{10} + n_{01},\; 0)$), and for this table $p(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = 1$, so $T(\boldsymbol{n}) \in \mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{n})$.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)-(S6). Lemma A.2 (p. 18): 'Let $n = 2m$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. For any potential outcome table $\boldsymbol{w}$, the pmf of $T(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Z})$ is symmetric about $\mathbb{E}[T(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Z})]$' (target P003-T24). Proof of Lemma 3.1 (p. 19): 'Let $\boldsymbol{w}$ be the potential outcome table provided by Lemma A.3, so that $\tau(\boldsymbol{w}) = T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ and $\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}) = \mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$. Then the distribution of $T(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Z})$ is symmetric about $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$, so $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$ is the median of the distribution. Then by (2.12), we have $p(\boldsymbol{w},\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) = 1$, which shows that $\tau(\boldsymbol{w})$ will always be accepted in Algorithm 2.3.'
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statement (first half of headline claim P003-H2); checked by a reader for balanced n <= 20. The companion footnote 9, which shows the claim can fail in an unbalanced design, has wrong numbers; its corrected form is target P003-T21. Since tau(w) = T(Y,Z) for the table of Lemma A.3, the observed deviation in (2.12) is zero and p = 1 directly.

canonical_claim.location: p. 7 (PDF p. 7); proof in Appendix A.3, p. 19 (PDF p. 19)
canonical_claim.statement:
'Proposition 3.3. Fix $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ with $m < n$, $\alpha \in (0,1)$, and true potential outcomes $\boldsymbol{y}$. For every $\boldsymbol{n} \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^{\{0,1\}^2}$, we have $|\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})| \le \sqrt{\frac{4}{\alpha} \cdot \frac{n}{n-1} \cdot \frac{n}{m(n-m)}}$. (3.3)'
[$|\mathcal{I}_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})| = U_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n}) - L_\alpha(\boldsymbol{n})$; $\boldsymbol{n}$ ranges over the observed count vectors of the design ($n_{11} + n_{10} = m$, $n_{01} + n_{00} = n - m$), the interval being defined when $\mathcal{K}(\boldsymbol{n}) \ne \varnothing$.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)-(S6). Steps of the printed proof (p. 19), for an arbitrary table $\boldsymbol{w}$ with $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}}$, $\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}$ as in Definition 2.1: 'By Imbens and Rubin (2015, Equation (6.3)), $\mathrm{Var}(T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}})) \le \frac{S_1^2}{m} + \frac{S_0^2}{n-m}$, (A.11) where $S_1^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(w_i(1) - \overline{w}(1))^2$, $\overline{w}(1) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i(1)$, (A.12) $S_0^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(w_i(0) - \overline{w}(0))^2$, $\overline{w}(0) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i(0)$. (A.13) Since the $w_i(j)$ are each 0 or 1, we have $S_1^2 \le \frac{n}{n-1}$, $S_0^2 \le \frac{n}{n-1}$ (A.14) and hence $\mathrm{Var}(T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}})) \le \frac{n^2}{n-1} \cdot \frac{1}{m(n-m)}$. (A.15) Let $V$ denote the quantity on the right-hand side of (A.15). Then Chebyshev's inequality implies that $\mathbb{P}(|T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}) - \tau(\boldsymbol{w})| \ge t) \le \frac{V}{t^2}$, (A.16) where we used that $T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}})$ has mean $\tau(\boldsymbol{w})$. We introduce the shorthand $\delta = |T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z}) - \tau(\boldsymbol{w})|$. (A.17) To reject $\boldsymbol{w}$, we must have $\mathbb{P}(|T(\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Y}},\widetilde{\boldsymbol{Z}}) - \tau(\boldsymbol{w})| \ge \delta) < \alpha$. (A.18) Using (A.16), we note that $V\delta^{-2} < \alpha$ is a sufficient condition for rejection. We solve $V\delta^{-2} < \alpha$ to find $\delta > \sqrt{V/\alpha}$. (A.19) Therefore the permutation test will reject all values of $\tau(\boldsymbol{w})$ with distance greater than $V^{1/2}\alpha^{-1/2}$ from $T(\boldsymbol{Y},\boldsymbol{Z})$.'
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample bound (second half of headline claim P003-H2). It gives the rate the text describes ('the intervals converge at a n^{-1/2} rate when m is proportional to n'): if c <= m/n <= 1 - c with 0 < c <= 1/2 and n >= 2, the right side of (3.3) is at most sqrt(8/(alpha c (1-c) n)). The exact finite-population facts used are E[T(w,Z)] = tau(w) and the variance bound (A.11), which follows from the Neyman variance formula Var(T) = S_1^2/m + S_0^2/(n-m) - S_{10}^2/n with S_{10}^2 >= 0 the sample variance of the unit effects. Footnote 10 says the constant is deliberately conservative. The mention of the true potential outcomes y in the statement is not used: the bound is for every observed count vector.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 4.2 (monotonicity of the permutation p-value along the line (4.3) in a balanced design)
canonical_claim.location: p. 8 (PDF p. 8); proof in Appendix B.3, pp. 21-25 (PDF pp. 21-25)
canonical_claim.statement:
'Lemma 4.2. Suppose $n = 2m$. Fix observed data $\boldsymbol{n}$, and a count vector $\boldsymbol{v} = (v_{11}, v_{10}, v_{01}, v_{00})$. Suppose $\min(v_{10},v_{01}) \ge 1$ and $\max(v_{10},v_{01}) \ge 2$, and set $\boldsymbol{v}' = (v_{11}+1,\; v_{10}-1,\; v_{01}-1,\; v_{00}+1)$. (4.3) Then $p(\boldsymbol{v}',\boldsymbol{n}) \ge p(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{n})$.'
[The count vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ has $v_{11}+v_{10}+v_{01}+v_{00} = n$ and need not be possible given $\boldsymbol{n}$; $\boldsymbol{n}$ is any observed count vector with $n_{11}+n_{10} = n_{01}+n_{00} = m$.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $p(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{n})$: Definition 2.1, standing assumption (S5). The paper's proof (p. 25): 'This is an immediate consequence of combining Lemmas B.12 and B.4.' Lemma B.4 (p. 21): 'Fix observed data $\boldsymbol{n}$, and a count vector $\boldsymbol{v} = (v_{11},v_{10},v_{01},v_{00})$. (B.14) Suppose $\min(v_{10},v_{01}) \ge 1$, and define $\boldsymbol{v}' = (v_{11}+1, v_{10}-1, v_{01}-1, v_{00}+1)$. (B.15) Set $\boldsymbol{v}^{\circ} = (v_{11}, v_{10}-1, v_{01}-1, v_{00})$, (B.16) and suppose that the pmf of $T(\boldsymbol{v}^{\circ},\boldsymbol{Z})$ is SD on the lattice $(m-1)^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$, where here $\boldsymbol{Z}$ is uniformly distributed over $\mathcal{Z}(n-2)$. Then $p(\boldsymbol{v}',\boldsymbol{n}) \ge p(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{n})$. (B.17)' Lemma B.12 (p. 25): 'Let $n = 2m$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$. Fix any potential outcome count vector $\boldsymbol{v} = (v_{11},v_{10},v_{01},v_{00})$, (B.56) and suppose $v_{10} + v_{01} \ge 1$. Then the pmf of $T(\boldsymbol{v},\boldsymbol{Z})$ is SD on $m^{-1}\mathbb{Z}$.' (Applied to $\boldsymbol{v}^{\circ}$, with $n - 2$ subjects and $v^{\circ}_{10} + v^{\circ}_{01} = v_{10} + v_{01} - 2 \ge 1$.) SD: Definition A.1, standing assumption (S13), in the corrected form of target P003-T14.
canonical_claim.note: Exact finite-sample statement: the 'new monotonicity property of the permutation p-value' of headline claim P003-H3. Checked by a reader for balanced n <= 26 (and Lemma B.12 for balanced n <= 40). Several steps of its proof chain have local errors whose corrected forms are separate targets: Definition A.1 (P003-T14), Lemma B.5 and its use in Lemma B.9 (P003-T9, P003-T10), the induction of Lemma B.12 (P003-T15), the displays (B.47)-(B.51) (P003-T16); none changes the lemma. The validator of P003-E008 gives an independent proof of Lemma B.12 for all balanced n.
